activity_context.topic_title: Integration by Substitution With Inverse Trigonometric Functions

feedback.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $2{x}^{2}=(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{2}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{1+2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =4\int \frac{1}{1+(\sqrt{2}x)^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{2}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
